newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat meets Israeli defence chief.
newsitem.headline: Arafat meets Israeli defence chief.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai met on Wednesday only hours after news that Mordechai had approved expansion of a West Bank Jewish settlement.
Palestinian and Israeli security men crowded around Mordechai as he emerged from his car to be greeted by Arafat at Beit Hanoun. A helicopter clattered overhead as the two men went inside.
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross said earlier on Wednesday that Jewish settlement was a "problem" after talks with Arafat in Gaza.

"The American policy on settlement activity has not changed. We continue to see it as a problem. We continue to see it as the kind of activity that complicates the negotiating process," Ross told reporters as he stood beside Arafat.
Arafat said: "No doubt this decision which has been taken by Mr Mordechai concerning building new houses is another breaching to what has been agreed upon and what has been signed."
News had just emerged that Mordechai had approved the building of an additional 1,800 housing units in a West Bank Jewish settlement.

PLO officials said Arafat planned to urge Mordechai at their meeting to carry out a troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron and stop settlement expansion on lands where Palestinians hope one day to establish a state.
Israel's Channel One television said Mordechai would only present Arafat with general principles guiding his government's approach to the Hebron issue.
Ross arrived in Gaza after talks in Egypt. He was to meet Israeli officials on Thursday.

"I think one of the things we both agreed on...was the importance to work as quickly as possible to get tangible results to translate the agenda that was agreed upon into real results that can be felt on the ground," Ross said.

Arafat, who doubts the commitment of the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, elected in May, to peace deals cut with Israel's previous administration, emphasised the agreements were signed under U.S. auspices.
"Not to forget that the peace agreement had been signed under the supervision of President Clinton and the White House and America was one of the sponsors," he said.
Mordechai is the architect of a new redeployment plan for Hebron likely to leave more Israeli troops in the city than was envisaged in the agreement signed by the previous government.
Netanyahu has said changes are necessary to ensure security for the 400 Jews who have settled among more than 100,000 Palestinians in Hebron.
"If Mordechai submits requests for changing the agreement, we will refuse because we reject renegotiating or modifying any signed agreement," said Arafat aide Tayeb Abdel-Rahim.
The redeployment, scheduled for last March, was postponed by the previous government after Moslem suicide bombers killed 59 people in Israel.

Hebron is the last of eight West Bank cities to be handed over to Palestinians under an interim PLO-Israel peace deals. Israel has also missed a September 7 date for initiating further redeployments from parts of the West Bank.
